There are a few types of stable orbits around a binary star system:

  • Orbit outside both the stars, so far away that you can almost treat them as a single gravity source. Like this accretion disk here.
  • Orbit around one star, so close that you can almost treat the other star as outside the system. Like this crappy picture here.

The best way to think of this is as the planet forms - it begins as dust, so before you get a planet you have to have a stable disk. The kinds of accretion disks that can form are strongly dependent on the size of the stars and their distance from each other - there's an instability region between the two stars where no stable orbits are possible because of the changing gravity as they orbit. (There are two accretion disks in that first image. The closer one will probably never form a planet, because the stars' motion will constantly tear the pieces apart. The larger one further out is more likely to be stable and 'quiet' enough to form a planet.)
